The Orinoco saltator (Saltator orenocensis) is a passerine bird inhabiting gallery forests and semi-deciduous woodlands of northern South America. Recently measured values of its basal metabolic rate, obtained via open-flow respirometry on rested adults during their inactive phase, reveal a resting oxygen consumption of 56.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 56.5 milliliters per hour] at a core body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This metabolic level, recorded under thermoneutral conditions, falls within the range typical for medium-sized emberizids. Newly hatched chicks emerge from the egg at a very modest size, with an initial wet body mass averaging 3.8 grams [Ww0 = 3.8 grams], a figure derived from comparative data within the genus. This small mass reflects the altricial state of the hatchling, which relies entirely on its parents for warmth and food during the first days of life. The rapid growth that ensues requires a substantial energetic subsidy from the provisioning adults over the subsequent nestling period.

Data on the typical incubation period for this species have been inferred from closely related members of the genus Saltator, particularly S. maximus. The duration from oviposition to hatching, when eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], is approximately 13.5 days [ab = approximately 13.5 days]. This developmental period is consistent with that of other tropical passerines, which generally exhibit slower embryonic development compared to temperate-zone counterparts. The stable thermal environment provided by the incubating adult is critical for successful embryogenesis, and any sustained deviation from this optimal temperature can compromise hatching success. Following hatching, the nestling enters a phase of rapid feather development and mass gain, entirely dependent on regurgitated food brought by both parents. The timing of these early life events is tightly linked to the local thermal regime, which in turn influences the availability of invertebrate prey necessary for chick growth.

Under the average active-phase body temperature maintained by adults and growing nestlings of this species, which is approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a consistent sequence of post-hatching milestones has been documented. Young birds first achieve the ability to sustain flight and depart the nest at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling phase compared to many other members of the family Thraupidae at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid fledging period may represent an adaptation to high nest predation pressure typical of Neotropical environments. After leaving the nest, the fledglings remain dependent on their parents for food for several additional weeks, gradually developing their foraging skills. The energetic demands during this period are substantial, as the juveniles must complete their growth and molt into adult plumage before their first breeding season. The pace of these developmental events is critical for survival and future reproductive success.

Sexual maturation in this species, as inferred from the commencement of gametogenesis and gonadal development, occurs at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at the species' typical body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This represents a relatively fast progression to physiological reproductive capability, though actual breeding is deferred until a later age. The attainment of puberty marks the beginning of the individual's potential to contribute genetically to the next generation, but ecological and social constraints, such as territory establishment and mate acquisition, often delay actual reproduction. Females, in particular, must achieve a sufficient body condition to support the energetic costs of egg production and incubation. The ultimate wet body mass attained by adult females in this species is approximately 34.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 34.7 grams], a size that reflects the energetic demands of reproduction. Adult body mass is a key determinant of fecundity and survival in passerine birds.

Females typically lay a clutch of 2 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 2 eggs] and are capable of producing approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year] under favorable conditions, yielding a modest annual reproductive output. The population's first successful breeding event typically occurs at 474.5 days since birth [tR = 474.5 days since birth], when maintained at the standard body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between sexual maturity and first reproduction is common among tropical passerines, which often invest a longer period in learning foraging techniques and establishing a stable territory. The maximum recorded lifespan for the Orinoco saltator, based on field observations of banded individuals, is 10.4 years [am = 10.4 years] under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity, while substantial for a bird of its size, reflects the relatively low extrinsic mortality rates typical of tropical environments, where seasonality is less pronounced and predation pressure is balanced by dense cover. The life history strategy of this species is thus characterized by a slow pace of life, with deferred reproduction and low annual fecundity offset by high adult survival. For example, the combination of a 14-day fledging period and a 42-day age at sexual maturity suggests a developmental trajectory that prioritizes rapid early growth while deferring reproductive investment to a time when territorial ownership and foraging proficiency are well established, a trade-off seen in many thraupids that inhabit stable forest environments.
